claims.feature: real people kept off the page
claims.claim: Kay prefers a Valerius and Alixana based on Justinian and Theodora as an up-front admission that no one knows what the real people were like in private.
claims.source: Teresa Basinski Eckford, 'Parallel Universes: Guy Gavriel Kay reflects on twenty years of alternative history', Historical Novels Review (Nov 2004)
claims.quote: we have no idea what the ‘real’ people were like

claims.claim: Kay describes his world-building as variations on historical themes rather than create-from-scratch worlds.
claims.source: Teresa Basinski Eckford, 'Parallel Universes: Guy Gavriel Kay reflects on twenty years of alternative history', Historical Novels Review (Nov 2004)
claims.quote: variations on historical themes, not create-from-scratch worlds

claims.claim: Kay notes his first published work and awards were for poetry.
claims.source: Teresa Basinski Eckford, 'Parallel Universes: Guy Gavriel Kay reflects on twenty years of alternative history', Historical Novels Review (Nov 2004)
claims.quote: My first published work was poetry

claims.claim: Kay says several scenes in Children of Earth and Sky narrate one conversation from more than one participant and the conversation is not the same.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books (2016-08-14)

claims.claim: Kay says the two moons declare 'We're not here', setting the rules of engagement with the reader.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books (2016-08-14)
claims.quote: The two moons say, We’re not here.

claims.claim: Kay says Children of Earth and Sky takes place in the lives of not-powerful people on the borderlands for whom emperors' ambitions matter little.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books (2016-08-14)
claims.quote: in the lives of not-powerful people

claims.claim: Kay says the fantastic lets him present the world as characters believe it, matter-of-factly, removing the modern reader's smugness (his definition of magic realism).
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books (2016-08-14)
claims.quote: the world is presented as the characters believe it to be

claims.claim: Kay calls the past staggeringly alien and criticises commercial historical writing that turns on relatability.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books (2016-08-14)

claims.feature: invisible seam between fact and invention
claims.claim: Kay says if a reader can pick out what is made up from what is real, the storytelling is botched.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books (2016-08-14)

claims.claim: The interviewer characterises Kay's prose as poetic and steeped in myth, with a reverence for language running through everything.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books (2016-08-14)
claims.quote: A reverence for language runs through everything he writes

claims.claim: The interviewer states all Kay's novels are told from multiple points of view, some scenes from several characters in turn; Kay declines to call this a comment on who tells history.
claims.source: Christine Fischer Guy, 'The Fantastic Worlds of Guy Gavriel Kay', Los Angeles Review of Books (2016-08-14)
claims.quote: Some scenes are told from several characters’ points of view

claims.claim: Kay says the quarter turn acknowledges from the outset that we cannot get history exactly right, an awareness reader and author share.
claims.source: Chris Urie, 'The Quarter Turn of History: A Conversation with Guy Gavriel Kay', Clarkesworld 117 (June 2016) — read via Wayback copy (live site is behind a JS challenge)
claims.quote: we can’t get it exactly right

claims.claim: Kay says five protagonists all move to the centre in different parts of the narrative and balancing them is a core task.
claims.source: Chris Urie, 'The Quarter Turn of History: A Conversation with Guy Gavriel Kay', Clarkesworld 117 (June 2016) — read via Wayback copy (live site is behind a JS challenge)
claims.quote: all move to the center in different parts

claims.claim: Kay wanted a book that felt epic against a great war but was about non-powerful men and women getting on with their lives.
claims.source: Chris Urie, 'The Quarter Turn of History: A Conversation with Guy Gavriel Kay', Clarkesworld 117 (June 2016) — read via Wayback copy (live site is behind a JS challenge)
claims.quote: non-powerful men and women trying to get on

claims.claim: Kay never wants a character or event to map directly onto a real one; history rhymes rather than repeats.
claims.source: 'Guy Gavriel Kay: Margins of History', Locus (May 2025 excerpt) — read via Wayback copy
